message.content: {"summary":"Your report has a logical spine and good use of external cases (HSSIB, Volkswagen, EACE), and your stakeholder framing in the Introduction is sound. To move up, you need an abstract (~150 words), a decision framework for shipping known-defect products, and consistency between your conclusion and your recommendations. Several claims need sourcing and your EACE clause citations need verifying.","next_steps":["Add a ~150-word abstract stating the scenario, the ethical question, your method, your conclusion (Not Ship) and your headline recommendations, so it matches your body rather than sitting apart from it.","Resolve the contradiction between your conclusion and your RECOMMENDATION section: make Recommendation 1 consistent with Not Ship (e.g. negotiate a delay or staged release rather than simply accepting the contract), and attach cost, risk and mitigation to each recommendation so the trade-offs are visible.","Build an explicit decision framework (e.g. criteria such as severity and detectability of the defect, number of users exposed, reversibility, disclosure and consent, contractual and legal obligations) and apply it to Rachel's case; source or remove the 1% failure estimate and check every EACE clause number against the actual code wording."],"criteria":{"C1":"You identify several issues and name Rachel, the company, the chip contractor and the health department, and you link quality-versus-competitiveness to engineering design. The stakeholder treatment is brief and generic, and the physical-harm versus data-loss distinction never gets framed here. For Excellent, say explicitly why each issue matters in an engineering organisation and trace each stakeholder's interest, exposure and power.","C2":"Your for-and-against structure is clear and readable, but the 'for shipping' case is thin and rests on unsupported assertions such as the company surviving and gaining competitive advantage. The health department and end clients are not given their own decision recommendations. For Very good and above, develop the strongest version of the opposing case and close with separate recommendations for Rachel, her company, the client and affected users.","C3":"Your report moves logically from arguments to the conclusion that shipping risks outweigh short-term benefit, and that reasoning is visible to the reader. The recommendation to accept the contract undercuts it, and stakeholder coverage is uneven. For Excellent, ensure every recommendation follows from the conclusion and show each stakeholder's position systematically through the argument.","C4":"The HSSIB and Volkswagen cases and the EACE code give your argument real grounding, and you reason from them rather than just citing them. The 1% figure is unsourced, the Apple/CNBC source is weakly tied to your point, and the HSSIB analogy to physical harm needs qualification. Add quantitative evidence and qualify the causal claim. For Excellent, pair qualitative and quantitative evidence throughout and assess each source's relevance to server defects specifically.","C5":"Sections are clearly divided and the writing is generally fluent, but the missing abstract is a structural gap, the heading 'DICUSSION' and 'Actin' are typos, and references [3] and [4] are incomplete with inconsistent Harvard/IEEE style. Add at least one table or figure (e.g. a stakeholder-impact matrix or decision tree). For Excellent, proofread, make citation style uniform and use several visual elements."}}
